Question: On May 29, the Office of the US Trade Representative held a hearing on the 301 investigation of China's maritime, logistics and shipbuilding industries, and many parties opposed the imposition of tariffs before the meeting. What do you think?
Old_Answer: The problem is the remedy proposed, which is the imposition of a docking fee in all US port of calls, targeting China-built ships exclusively. The remedy aims to collect at least $1m per ship docking (calibrated to the cost of goods carried) to feed a fund benefiting shipbuilding and metalworking unions. That’s robbing Peter to pay Paul, and unprecedented. It is also illegal, because of the brazen, targeted nature, just like the blanket tariffs announced under Donald. That is why the WTO’s dispute settlement mechanism remains paralyzed. This is also a tariff on tariff for goods originating from China carried on board China-built ships, because of the blanket tariff already in place. Where is this going to end? Are they going after China-built containers next, imposing a handling fee for every container based on cost of goods carried? I won’t be surprised if this passes, because America is willing to throw in the kitchen sink just to “win”. It will stop at nothing, not even general war. Is it a good idea, economically? No, because it will reshape trade flow, while China-built ships maintain a healthy economic edge over rivals. It just adds to the cost of doing business with the US, making the consumer pay more to benefit the pockets of a small number of union workers, funding the retirement of baby boomers. There is no way to revitalize ocean-going shipbuilding stateside with the cost structure today. The Jones Act, after all, dates back to 1920, and what has a century of protectionism bought?

Question: Are you convinced by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's argument that the ringgit's decline does not reflect the reality of Malaysia's strengthening economy?
Old_Answer: That’s a departure from Mahathir’s horror almost 30 years ago, when he complained loudly about the currency turmoil during the AFC that WIPED OUT TWO DECADES OF GROWTH IN TWO WEEKS, with Malaysia losing billions in purchasing power. The devaluation of the ringgit is structural and has been ongoing for 4 decades. In 1980, Singapore was still in a currency union with Malaysia. The SGD was 1:1 with the MYR. Today, it is >3.5, the lowest it has ever been. Is it a floor? I don’t think so. Malaysia is styling itself as a cheaper alternative to China in some sectors, and growth has mostly been padded by forex, particularly the reverse plaza accord over the past decade. Otherwise, the Malaysia today is not too different from the Malaysia of the 2000s, competitive advantage wise. Is Malaysia climbing out of covid? Certainly. But is it clawing back lost decades? Question: Did the U.S. Commerce Department tech sanctions on China spark the fall in Intel’s share price and decision to lay off 15k employees?
Old_Answer: Well, dell is on course to lay off 25k staff this year and last. Dell's employee count is in the same low 100k bracket as Intel. Evidently, there has been a huge squeeze on the x86 ecosystem the past 2 years. My friend recently returned from a stateside trip to survey investment opportunities. I asked him about Intel and he said it wasn't on his shortlist of blue chip picks. His homework? Go through the Financials. Here're some numbers. Intel's revenue is down 30% last year compared to the pandemic driven peak of 2020-2021. That's a 24b hole. Now, the US GDP was 20t in 2017. Last year, it was 27t, a 35% increase, with a big chunk of it inflation driven. The problem for Intel? It brought in less revenue in 2023 compared to 2017! Intel has a peculiar way of reporting geographical revenue. It divides the pie into 5 parts. China, US, rest of the world, Singapore and Taiwan, sorted for size. Intel sells 3x as many chips to China, Singapore and Taiwan compared to the rest of the world ex-US. Surprised? The problem with Intel is structural, and it goes to the heart of the business model. Intel is vertically integrated. It is not only a chip designer, it is also a chip fabricator. Whereas everyone else is fabless today, and the list includes Nvidia, qualcomm and apple. Intel used to have defacto control of chipmaking tools and marerials, because it had the biggest budget at the head of the x86 monopoly. Unfortunately, the iPhone and arm changed the status quo irrevocably. Revenue from Apple and Android supercharged the contract manufacturing of chips, and within 6-8 years of the iphone's introduction, tsmc overhauled intel's lead as the owner of the leading edge process node. The best chipmaking tools were now offered to tsmc and Samsung, as Intel failed to find its lost mojo. There are reports of abnormal processor failure rates in the latest 13th and 14th generation products, which have affected the revenue of system builders. Promises made in the past few years by management regarding tech leadership and expansion have fallen flat. All told, it is a tale of a company in crisis, and cost cutting mode, rather than the confident growth of a company enabled by CHIPS act grants and loans. Now back to China. The Chinese government has ordered all departments to transition away from Microsoft and Intel products, due to the growing risk of sanctions crippling their work flow. Chinese companies are heeding the call as well, especially after Dell's politically motivated withdrawal from manufacturing in china. Then again, the top xeon processors have been banned from sale in China for many years. Together with the move towards gpu powered ai data centers, and the growing realization of windows on ARM, it has been a triple whammy for Intel, as its rug is pulled on its most profitable ecosystems (servers and mobile content creation). So yes, Intel has been hurt by toxic American politics, but its problems go deeper than that. Intel's business model hasn't kept up with the shifting sands of the chip market and is in danger of obsolescence.

Old_Answer: The BRI is more than a decade old. Currently, >150 nations have expressed interest in boarding the BRI train, and participation at meetings in Beijing have been increasing. That is ok, because Italy is sovereign, and it takes two to clap. However, it will lose real projects that are hard-to-replace bargains, which could have helped Italy’s connectivity and economic growth. And China is ok with that. There is more than enough business and projects to explore with 150 partners, way more than China has the resources for. Earlier projects nearing completion/handover are the perfect advertisement, especially as they drive economic growth and bring prosperity to underserved populations, repeating what has happened throughout China. This will hammer home the fact the Chinese are here to stay, and are fully capable of delivering on agreed terms. Italy is what, 60m? The global south is 7b, a >100x multiple. Italy gets to demonstrate solidarity and exemplary values, while China doesn’t lose sleep over “lost business”. Looks like a win-win. Note: The I in BRI is short for Initiative. It isn’t an alliance or bloc. This is merely a gathering of nations to coordinate and propose infrastructure projects that increase CONNECTIVITY between destinations, and it can be domestic or cross-border in scope.
